questions.stem: Which list contains only abiotic factors?

options.text: Temperature, light intensity and wind speed
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Predation, competition and disease
options.explanation: All three are living pressures, so biotic.

options.text: Food supply and pathogens
options.explanation: Food and pathogens involve living organisms.

options.text: Grazing and pollination
options.explanation: Grazing and pollination are biotic interactions.

questions.stem: What defines a biotic factor?

options.text: It is any factor humans measure
options.explanation: Measurement has nothing to do with the split.

options.text: It is a living pressure in the environment
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It is any chemical in the soil
options.explanation: Chemicals alone are abiotic; life defines biotic.

options.text: It is weather measured daily
options.explanation: Weather is non-living, so abiotic.

questions.stem: Wind speed over a sand dune is which kind of factor?

options.text: Biotic, because plants respond to it
options.explanation: Responses do not make the factor living.

options.text: Neither category applies
options.explanation: Wind speed is a textbook abiotic factor.

options.text: Abiotic, because wind is non-living
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Biotic, because it moves living sand grains
options.explanation: Sand is not alive; wind stays abiotic.

questions.stem: Ash dieback disease sweeping through a woodland is which factor?

options.text: Abiotic, because spores are tiny
options.explanation: Size does not decide; the fungus is living.

options.text: Abiotic, because weather spreads spores
options.explanation: Weather only carries the living cause.

options.text: Neither, disease is human-made
options.explanation: Natural disease is a classic biotic factor.

options.text: Biotic, because a living pathogen drives it
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: Why do ecologists separate the two factor families?

options.text: Because living and non-living pressures shape populations through different mechanisms
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Because one family matters more always
options.explanation: Both matter; the split is about mechanism.

options.text: Because exams demand two lists
options.explanation: The split reflects real ecological causation.

options.text: Because factors never interact
options.explanation: They interact constantly; classification aids analysis.

questions.stem: State the meaning of the term abiotic factor.
questions.modelAnswer: An abiotic factor is a non-living part of the environment, such as temperature or light intensity.

questions.stem: State the meaning of the term biotic factor.
questions.modelAnswer: A biotic factor is a living pressure within the environment, such as competition, predation or disease.

questions.stem: Explain why light intensity is classed as abiotic while food supply is biotic.
questions.modelAnswer: Light intensity is abiotic because light is non-living, while food supply is biotic because the food is made of living or once-living organisms.

questions.stem: A drought dries a pond while herons arrive to fish. Classify both pressures.
questions.modelAnswer: The drought is abiotic, being a non-living water shortage, while the herons are biotic, being living predators on the pond organisms.

questions.stem: Why does low light shrink a woodland food chain from the bottom?

options.text: Because soil washes away
options.explanation: Soil loss is a separate factor.

options.text: Because photosynthesis slows, so plants yield less food for herbivores
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Because herbivores dislike shade
options.explanation: The effect starts with plant growth, not herbivore taste.

options.text: Because light kills insects
options.explanation: Light does not kill insects at low intensity.

questions.stem: How does temperature act on survival?

options.text: It only matters to reptiles
options.explanation: All organisms carry enzymes affected by temperature.

options.text: It affects plants but never animals
options.explanation: Animal enzymes are just as temperature-sensitive.

options.text: It sets the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions, and extremes reduce survival
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It changes the number of bones
options.explanation: Skeletal counts do not shift with temperature.

questions.stem: Why can cacti store water in deserts while amphibians cannot?

options.text: Cacti drink morning dew faster
options.explanation: Water storage and reduced loss are the stated adaptations.

options.text: Amphibians fear sunlight only
options.explanation: Moisture for reproduction is the deciding factor.

options.text: Deserts lack predators for cacti
options.explanation: Predation is not the mechanism here.

options.text: Cacti store water and cut losses, while amphibians need moist conditions to reproduce
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: What happens to fish in warm stagnant ponds?

options.text: Oxygen drops, so fish die or migrate to better-oxygenated water
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Fish grow extra gills
options.explanation: No anatomical change is described.

options.text: Fish switch to breathing air
options.explanation: Fish cannot simply switch to air breathing.

options.text: The pond becomes saltier
options.explanation: Salinity is a different abiotic factor.

questions.stem: Why do lichens indicate clean air?

options.text: Because lichens grow only in cities
options.explanation: They thrive in clean air, the opposite.

options.text: Because sulfur dioxide pollution removes them, so their presence signals clean air
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Because lichens feed on pollution
options.explanation: Pollution kills them; they do not feed on it.

options.text: Because lichens need city noise
options.explanation: Noise is irrelevant to lichens.

questions.stem: State one abiotic factor that affects plant growth in forests.
questions.modelAnswer: Light intensity affects plant growth, since low light slows photosynthesis and reduces the food available to herbivores.

questions.stem: Name the abiotic factor that limits polar bears to cold regions.
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature limits polar bears to cold regions, where their thick fur and fat layer suit survival.

questions.stem: Explain why soil pH shapes which plants grow on moorland.
questions.modelAnswer: Soil pH shapes plant growth because acidic moorland suits heather while grasses and many crops fail, which then decides which animals the habitat can feed.

questions.stem: A factory releases sulfur dioxide near a woodland. Predict the lichen population.
questions.modelAnswer: The lichen population falls because lichens are sensitive to sulfur dioxide, so polluted air removes them while tolerant species persist.

questions.stem: What happens to a population when its food supply rises?

options.text: Only predators benefit
options.explanation: The fed species itself gains first.

options.text: Nothing changes without rain
options.explanation: Food supply itself shifts population size.

options.text: Survival and reproduction improve, so the population increases
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The population falls as crowding spreads disease
options.explanation: More food supports more organisms, not fewer.

questions.stem: Why did the grey squirrel population push red squirrels into decline after arriving in the UK?

options.text: They hunted red squirrels directly
options.explanation: Competition and disease, not direct hunting, drove the decline.

options.text: They ate all the acorns before ripening
options.explanation: Wider food use, including unripe acorns, gave the advantage.

options.text: They poisoned the water supply
options.explanation: Water poisoning is not the documented mechanism.

options.text: They take food and nesting sites from red squirrels and carry a virus
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: What made ash dieback disease so damaging for populations in Europe?

options.text: Ash populations had no resistance to the newly arrived fungus
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Ash trees were already dying of drought
options.explanation: Drought is not the cause named for dieback spread.

options.text: The fungus killed all other trees too
options.explanation: The named host is ash, not every species.

options.text: Foresters planted infected seeds on purpose
options.explanation: Deliberate planting is not part of the account.

questions.stem: When does the losing competitor face local extinction?

options.text: When food becomes unlimited
options.explanation: Unlimited food would ease, not cause, extinction.

options.text: When its numbers fall too low to breed successfully
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: As soon as any competitor appears
options.explanation: Decline takes hold as competition bites, not instantly.

options.text: Only if humans remove it
options.explanation: The losing species can fade without human help.

questions.stem: Red foxes were introduced to Australia for hunting. Which population declined as the new predator spread?

options.text: Foxes died out from the heat
options.explanation: Foxes established and spread widely.

options.text: Nothing changed for decades
options.explanation: The introduction caused marked declines.

options.text: Native small mammals and birds declined as the new predator spread
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Native species adopted foxes as prey
options.explanation: Foxes are the predators, not the prey.

questions.stem: State one biotic factor that changes population size.
questions.modelAnswer: Competition is a biotic factor, and the better-adapted species outcompetes the other, changing population size.

questions.stem: Name the biotic factor illustrated by a new fungus entering a woodland.
questions.modelAnswer: A new pathogen is the biotic factor, since the fungus infects populations with no resistance.

questions.stem: Explain why a new predator hits prey harder than an established one.
questions.modelAnswer: A new predator hits harder because the prey population has no shared history of balance with it, so numbers fall before any equilibrium forms.

questions.stem: Grey squirrels carry a virus red squirrels resist poorly. State two pressures on red squirrels.
questions.modelAnswer: Red squirrels face competition for food and nesting sites plus disease from the virus, so both biotic pressures drive their decline.
